# title: ENG-205 Early 17th Century (1603-1660) — 1 Main Ideas Pathway (play in order)
# short: 1 Main Ideas Pathway (play in order)

column2: Childless Elizabeth I died in 1603 and her relative James Stuart, James VI of Scotland, became James I, first putting England and Scotland under one ruler.
The Elizabethan period (1558-1603) is named for Elizabeth, the Jacobean (1603-1625) for James from Latin Jacobus, and the Caroline (1625-1640) for Charles from Latin Carolus.

column1: 03. Divine right breeds conflict (State and Church)
column2: James I believed kings got their power from God, not the people, and his illegal taxes to pay for a lavish court built tension with Parliament that ended with Charles I's beheading in 1649.
James's 1604 peace with Spain made the Atlantic safe, which led to Jamestown, Caribbean settlements, and the East India Company's first Indian outpost in 1611.

column1: 05. Toleration ends with a plot (State and Church)
column2: James's move toward religious toleration stopped after the 1605 Gunpowder Plot, in which Catholics tried to blow up Parliament, renewing anti-Catholic feeling.
The most important religious event of James's reign was his elegant, diplomatic translation known as the King James Bible.

column1: 07. Charles angers the Puritans (State and Church)
column2: Charles I's Catholic wife Henrietta Maria, love of ceremony, and appointment of Archbishop Laud, who taught that salvation was open to all through works, made Puritans suspect popery.
Writers like Donne, Burton, and Jonson still used the Ptolemaic universe, four elements, four humors, and the chain of being even as Harvey and Galileo challenged them.
Most writers still relied on patrons and manuscripts, but printing literature became more common after Ben Jonson printed his own works in a grand folio.
Jacobean writers moved to jagged, colloquial rhythms and short forms, led by Jonson's Tribe of Ben, Donne's metaphysical wit, and Herbert's religious verse.
Charles's court masques celebrated chivalry and royal love while Puritans like William Prynne attacked court excess and were brutally punished.
After Charles ruled more than ten years without Parliament, the 1640 Long Parliament refused to disband, executed Laud and Strafford, and civil war began in 1642.

column1: 13. A king put on trial (Revolutionary Era)
column2: The Rump Parliament tried and beheaded Charles I on 30 January 1649, overturning the idea that kings ruled by divine right.
Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector until 1658, his son Richard failed, and Parliament restored Charles II on May 8, 1660, but with limited monarchy.
Debates over the source of power, church government, and church-state relations produced religious toleration, freedom from censorship, and separation of church and state.
Parliament closed public theaters in 1642 and court patronage collapsed, so royalist writers worked in exile while Milton and Marvell supported the republic.
